algorithm.title: Clinical trial power and sample size assessment

nodes.text: Define null hypothesis (H0: no difference) and alternative hypothesis (H1: true difference)
Set acceptable error rates: alpha (type I error, 0.05) and beta (type II error, 0.10-0.20)
Calculate statistical power (1 - beta): probability of detecting a true effect when present
**Small sample size with large observed difference (p > 0.05):** study is underpowered to exclude false negative
**Adequately powered trial (large N):** tight confidence intervals confirm true equivalence or superiority
Perform a priori sample size calculation based on expected effect size before trial launch

algorithm.title: Diagnostic test accuracy: sensitivity and specificity

nodes.text: Diagnostic test evaluation: compare new test against established reference gold standard
Calculate sensitivity: true positives divided by all diseased individuals (TP / [TP + FN])
**Sensitivity in this study:** 81 positive tests out of 100 diseased patients yields 81%
Calculate specificity: true negatives divided by all non-diseased individuals (TN / [TN + FP])
**Specificity in this study:** 95 negative tests out of 100 control subjects yields 95%
False positive rate equals 1 minus specificity (5%); false negative rate equals 1 minus sensitivity (19%)

algorithm.title: Tetralogy of Fallot diagnosis and management

nodes.text: Infant with paroxysmal cyanosis during feeding/crying (tet spells) + systolic murmur: Tetralogy of Fallot

Definitive management: complete elective surgical repair with VSD patch and relief of obstruction

algorithm.title: Confounding and selection bias in clinical trials

nodes.text: Evaluate clinical trial design: distinguish observational cohort from randomized controlled trial
Treatment allocation at physician discretion: introduces selection bias (confounding by indication)
**Surgeon preference bias:** sicker patients or complex anatomy assigned to one graft type
Randomized allocation: essential method to balance known and unknown confounders between groups
Blinding (double-blind): prevents performance and assessment bias during follow-up
**Observational equivalence claims:** require propensity score matching or multivariable regression

abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.scope: screening recommendations (men 65-75 who smoked), ultrasound imaging, surveillance intervals, elective repair thresholds, rupture
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.core: Older adult with abdominal aortic dilation may remain asymptomatic until expansion or rupture; sudden abdominal/back pain and hypotension require immediate vascular rescue.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking strongest modifiable risk; older age, male sex, family history, hypertension, atherosclerosis
Women have higher rupture risk at smaller diameters; most aneurysms infrarenal

rows.label: Clues
items: Incidental pulsatile expansile abdominal mass; localized persistent pain suggests symptomatic aneurysm
Rupture triad incompletely present; transient stability may reflect contained retroperitoneal hemorrhage
Blue toe/distal ischemia may result from mural thrombus embolization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Medial elastin/collagen degradation → progressive enlargement; greater wall radius increases tension
Retroperitoneal containment can briefly limit blood loss before catastrophic decompensation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** diagnoses AAA, generally diameter ≥3 cm; no contrast required
★ Stable suspected rupture or preoperative planning → **CT angiography**
Unstable suspected rupture → bedside ultrasound if immediate; no CT transport delaying surgery
Ultrasound detects aneurysm but cannot reliably exclude rupture; follow symptoms/hemodynamics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Rupture → **urgent vascular repair**, IV access, blood products; avoid delaying for complete workup
Permissive hypotension during transfer/resuscitation until hemorrhage control when clinically feasible
★ Elective repair at **≥5.5 cm men, ≥5.0 cm women**, or aneurysm-attributable symptoms
Rapid growth ≥0.5 cm/6 months → repair consideration; endovascular versus open based on anatomy/fitness
Smaller asymptomatic lesions → ultrasound surveillance below; refer vascular surgery, manage cardiovascular risks

rows.label: Complications
items: Rupture, thrombosis, distal embolization; repair → AKI, bowel ischemia, endoleak after EVAR
Aortoenteric fistula after prior graft: herald GI bleed → catastrophic hemorrhage; urgent evaluation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **one-time ultrasound men 65–75 who ever smoked**; selectively screen never-smoking men
Women never smoked/no family history → no screening; women smokers/family history → USPSTF evidence insufficient
Smoking cessation, BP control, statin for atherosclerotic disease; lifelong imaging follow-up after EVAR

rows.label: Mimics
items: Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; shock atypical
Aortic dissection: abrupt chest/back pain, possible pulse deficits or branch ischemia

abdominal-trauma.name: Abdominal trauma
abdominal-trauma.scope: Blunt abdominal trauma (splenic/hepatic laceration, FAST exam, CT scan), penetrating abdominal trauma (stab, gunshot, peritonitis, exploratory laparotomy indications)
abdominal-trauma.core: Abdominal injury after collision, fall, stabbing, or gunshot: hemodynamic status and peritoneal signs determine imaging versus immediate operation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-speed deceleration, seat-belt compression, lower rib fractures; anticoagulation increases bleeding risk
Stab wounds may spare viscera; bullets frequently injure multiple structures

rows.label: Clues
items: LUQ pain or referred left shoulder pain → splenic injury; RUQ tenderness → hepatic injury
Distention, ecchymoses, abdominal wall marks; initially benign examination does not exclude bowel injury
★ **Rigidity, rebound, persistent hypotension**, or evisceration → urgent operative assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Solid-organ disruption → intraperitoneal hemorrhage; mesenteric injury → ischemia or delayed perforation
Retroperitoneal injury may produce little intraperitoneal free fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **FAST** at bedside during resuscitation; detects free fluid, not organ-specific injury
★ Stable → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast**; evaluate solid organs, bowel, retroperitoneum
Negative FAST with ongoing shock → search thorax/pelvis, repeat assessment; do not assume safety
Stable anterior stab → local wound exploration or serial examination/CT; trajectory guides evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, large-bore IV access, warmed blood products; massive transfusion for hemorrhagic shock
★ Unstable + positive FAST or peritonitis → **exploratory laparotomy**; no CT delay
Stable splenic/hepatic injury → monitored nonoperative care; arterial blush or persistent bleeding → angioembolization
Penetrating injury with enteric contents or uncontrolled bleeding → operation; selected stable cases permit observation
Suspected bowel perforation → ceftriaxone + metronidazole; early trauma surgery consultation

rows.label: Complications
items: Delayed splenic rupture, abscess, bile leak, abdominal compartment syndrome
Missed hollow-viscus injury → sepsis; splenectomy → overwhelming encapsulated bacterial infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Restraints, airbags, injury-prevention counseling
★ After splenectomy → **pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib vaccines**; fever requires urgent antibiotics

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pelvic hemorrhage: unstable pelvis, negative abdominal FAST
Tension pneumothorax: unilateral absent breath sounds, obstructive shock

acute-coronary-syndromes.name: Acute coronary syndromes
acute-coronary-syndromes.scope: Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, cardiac biomarkers, risk stratification (HEART/TIMI), antiplatelet and anticoagulation, reperfusion
acute-coronary-syndromes.core: Acute myocardial ischemia from coronary plaque disruption: distinguish occlusive infarction needing immediate reperfusion from non-ST-elevation syndromes needing risk-guided invasive management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, age, premature family CAD
Cocaine/stimulants, anemia, tachyarrhythmia may provoke ischemia; distinguish supply-demand injury from plaque rupture

rows.label: Clues
items: Pressure with arm/jaw radiation, diaphoresis, nausea; older adults/diabetes may have dyspnea alone
Inferior MI with hypotension, clear lungs, raised JVP → suspect RV infarction
★ New murmur, pulmonary edema, shock after MI → **mechanical complication**, urgent echo

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Platelet activation and thrombin-mediated clot reduce coronary perfusion; necrosis releases troponin
Type 2 MI: oxygen mismatch without acute atherothrombosis; treat precipitating cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG within 10 minutes**, repeat if nondiagnostic; serial high-sensitivity troponin using validated pathway
Posterior suspicion → V7–V9; inferior MI → right-sided leads; new LBBB alone insufficient for STEMI
★ **Do not wait for troponin before STEMI reperfusion**; bedside echo if diagnosis/complications uncertain
HEART ≤3 + negative serial troponins → low risk; TIMI/GRACE stratifies NSTE-ACS

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Chewed aspirin**, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant such as heparin, high-intensity atorvastatin; oxygen only if hypoxemic
Nitroglycerin for pain unless hypotension, RV infarction, or recent PDE5 inhibitor; avoid NSAIDs
★ STEMI → **primary PCI** within 90 minutes at PCI center, ≤120 minutes including transfer
IF PCI delay >120 minutes, symptoms <12 hours, no contraindication → fibrinolysis promptly, then transfer

rows.label: Complications
items: VT/VF, AV block, HF, cardiogenic shock; papillary rupture, septal rupture, free-wall rupture
Later aneurysm/thrombus, embolism, Dressler syndrome; antithrombotics → bleeding

rows.label: Prevention
items: DAPT usually 12 months after ACS unless bleeding risk changes plan; cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation
ACE inhibitor/ARB for LV dysfunction; beta-blocker when stable, avoid in shock or acute decompensation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic dissection: abrupt tearing pain/pulse deficit; anticoagulation or lysis dangerous
Pericarditis: positional pleuritic pain, diffuse changes
PE: hypoxemia, thrombotic risk, RV strain

Regional ST elevation or occlusion equivalent
Prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding, suspected dissection

acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Volume depletion, sepsis, heart failure, cirrhosis; baseline CKD increases vulnerability
NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion
Aminoglycosides, pigment injury, prolonged ischemia → tubular damage; antibiotics/PPIs → interstitial inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Oliguria, edema, uremic nausea; urine output may remain normal
AIN: fever, rash, eosinophilia sometimes present; classic triad often absent
★ Pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, encephalopathy, pericarditis → **urgent renal support**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced glomerular pressure, tubular epithelial injury, or backpressure → declining GFR

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ AKI: creatinine ↑≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, ≥1.5-fold within 7 days, or oliguria
Oliguria criterion: urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h; trend creatinine, electrolytes, fluid balance
★ **Urinalysis + microscopy**, medication review; bladder scan → renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
FeNa unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction; urine eosinophils neither sensitive nor specific
Unexplained persistent injury or suspected glomerulonephritis → nephrology, possible kidney biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe hyperkalemia → **IV calcium**, insulin/dextrose; refractory electrolyte disturbance → dialysis
Hypovolemia → isotonic crystalloid; congestion → loop diuretic; avoid reflex fluids in overloaded patients
Stop culprit nephrotoxins; renal-dose drugs; AIN persisting after withdrawal → consider glucocorticoids
★ Obstruction → **catheter or ureteral decompression**; monitor postobstructive diuresis
Dialysis: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, intoxication, overload, symptomatic uremia; no isolated creatinine threshold

rows.label: Complications
items: Arrhythmias, acidosis, volume overload; subsequent CKD
Recovery diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte losses

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain perfusion during illness; review nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function

rows.label: Mimics
items: CKD: longstanding abnormalities, small echogenic kidneys, chronic anemia
Trimethoprim effect: creatinine rise without true GFR decline

acute-kidney-injury.evidence: Not checked online; established KDIGO diagnostic criteria and renal teaching.

acute-respiratory-failure.name: Acute respiratory failure
acute-respiratory-failure.scope: Hypoxemic respiratory failure (type 1), hypercapnic respiratory failure (type 2), noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP), indications for invasive mechanical ventilation
acute-respiratory-failure.core: Acute inability to maintain oxygenation or ventilation demands simultaneous cause treatment and escalating respiratory support, guided by work of breathing and airway safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, ARDS, PE → oxygenation failure
COPD, neuromuscular weakness, obesity hypoventilation, sedatives → ventilation failure; overlap common

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachypnea, accessory-muscle use, hypoxemia, diaphoresis; hypercapnia may cause headache, somnolence, asterixis
★ **Exhaustion, declining consciousness, silent chest, paradoxical breathing** → impending respiratory arrest
Normal saturation on supplemental oxygen does not exclude dangerous CO₂ retention

rows.label: Pathophys
items: V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion impairment lowers PaO₂; shunt may resist oxygen alone
Inadequate alveolar ventilation raises PaCO₂; abrupt rise causes respiratory acidosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pulse oximetry + ABG** when severe distress, hypercapnia concern, or escalating support
Chest radiograph, ECG, bedside lung/cardiac ultrasound; infection/PE testing follows clinical context
Trend pH, gases, respiratory rate, mentation and effort; do not wait for an extreme number
Chronic compensated hypercapnia has elevated bicarbonate; pH decline identifies acute deterioration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oxygen immediately**, treat cause; target SpO₂ 88–92% with CO₂-retention risk, usually 92–96% otherwise
Hypoxemic failure needing more than conventional oxygen → high-flow nasal cannula, close reassessment
★ Awake cooperative COPD + respiratory acidosis → **BiPAP**; cardiogenic edema → CPAP/BiPAP plus diuresis/nitrates
★ **Intubate** for airway failure, refractory hypoxemia, shock, arrest, exhaustion, or worsening despite noninvasive support
Avoid NIV with vomiting, unprotected airway, copious secretions, major facial trauma; reassess within 1–2 h

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrhythmia, multiorgan failure; delayed intubation worsens outcome
Positive pressure → hypotension/barotrauma; invasive ventilation → pneumonia and ventilator-induced lung injury
Ventilated ARDS: low tidal volume using predicted body weight, limited plateau pressure; prone if severe

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, respiratory vaccination, disease control, cautious sedatives, aspiration precautions
High-risk extubation patients may benefit from planned NIV rather than rescue after deterioration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Metabolic acidosis: compensatory tachypnea with low CO₂
Panic hyperventilation: respiratory alkalosis without sustained gas-exchange failure

table.title: Gas-exchange classification; room air when feasible

acute-rhinosinusitis.name: Acute rhinosinusitis
acute-rhinosinusitis.scope: Common cold, viral rhinosinusitis, acute bacterial rhinosinusitis criteria, symptomatic therapy, antibiotic stewardship
acute-rhinosinusitis.core: Acute nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and facial pressure usually reflect a self-limited viral infection; duration and course identify likely bacterial disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Respiratory exposure, daycare contacts, impaired drainage from allergic inflammation
Immunocompromise, recent antibiotics, or hospitalization increases resistant-organism risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Cough, reduced smell, maxillary tenderness; colored mucus alone does not establish bacterial infection
★ Orbital swelling, painful eye movement, reduced vision, severe headache → **complicated infection**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral mucosal edema blocks sinus drainage; secondary infection commonly pneumococcus, H influenzae, or Moraxella

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; uncomplicated illness needs neither sinus radiographs nor CT
Persistent, severe, or biphasic course identifies bacterial cases; fever alone is insufficient
Suspected orbital/intracranial extension → contrast CT; MRI for intracranial definition
Refractory or unusual infection → ENT evaluation; routine nasal swab cultures unhelpful

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Viral illness → **saline irrigation, acetaminophen/NSAID**; no antibiotics
Intranasal fluticasone for associated allergic inflammation; topical oxymetazoline at most 3 days
★ Uncomplicated bacterial illness + reliable follow-up → **watchful waiting** or antibiotics
Antibiotic choice: amoxicillin-clavulanate, usually 5–7 days in adults; penicillin allergy → doxycycline
Complication → admission, IV ampicillin-sulbactam, urgent ENT/ophthalmology; avoid empiric azithromycin because resistance

rows.label: Complications
items: Orbital cellulitis or abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, intracranial abscess
Unnecessary antibiotics → diarrhea, C difficile, resistance

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, smoking avoidance, control allergic rhinitis
Sterile/distilled or previously boiled water for nasal irrigation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Allergic rhinitis: itching, sneezing, watery discharge without fever
Migraine: episodic disabling headache, photophobia, nausea
Dental infection: focal tooth pain, unilateral maxillary symptoms

table.title: Bacterial patterns
rows: Initial improvement → new fever or worsening symptoms

adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.name: Adolescent confidentiality and care
adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.scope: Confidentiality principles, exceptions to parental notification, parental requests for drug testing, encouraging family involvement
adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.core: Provide adolescents private, developmentally appropriate care; explain confidentiality and its safety limits before sensitive questions.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality supports honest disclosure; consent authority and parental access vary by jurisdiction
Assent: involve the adolescent even when guardian permission remains necessary

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Interview alone** for sexual health, substance use, mood, violence, and safety
★ Explain permitted confidential services; protect portals, billing, and result notifications
Encourage trusted-adult involvement; never require disclosure for legally confidential services

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ Parental request for **drug testing** → discuss concern, interview teen; avoid covert testing
Do not promise absolute secrecy or automatically send sensitive findings to parents

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Imminent danger, suspected **abuse/neglect/exploitation** → protective disclosure and reporting
Emergency treatment when delay risks serious harm; involve guardians when feasible
Emancipated minors generally self-consent; pregnancy alone does not universally confer emancipation

rows.label: Traps
items: Minor consent rules differ for STI, contraception, pregnancy, mental health, and substance treatment
Mandatory reporting thresholds for consensual sexual activity depend on ages and local law
Disclose minimum necessary information; explain safety-driven disclosure to adolescent whenever feasible

adolescent-confidentiality-and-care.evidence: Not checked online; established ethics principles; jurisdiction-specific consent/reporting law must be verified locally.

adult-immunizations.name: Adult immunizations
adult-immunizations.scope: Routine adult vaccines, immunocompromised and HIV, pregnancy, live-vaccine contraindications, chronic medical conditions (COPD, diabetes, liver disease), vaccine counseling and addressing hesitancy
adult-immunizations.core: Match vaccination to age, prior doses, pregnancy, immune status, and exposure risk; missed series resume without restarting.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ **HepB**: all adults 19–59; ≥60 with risk or requesting protection
Liver disease → HepA/HepB; COPD, diabetes, smoking → pneumococcal before routine age
Asplenia → pneumococcal, MenACWY, MenB, Hib; HIV → MenACWY

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Pregnancy: **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 wk**; inactivated influenza any trimester
Maternal RSV: Abrysvo at 32–36 wk, September–January; previous pregnancy dose → infant antibody instead
RSV once: all ≥75; ages 50–74 with increased severe-disease risk

rows.label: Test
items: Review records, contraindications, immunity; HBV serology useful, but **do not delay vaccination**
★ Immunocompromised ≥19 → recombinant zoster; HIV CD4 ≥200 permits MMR/varicella if nonimmune
HPV started <15 → two doses; ≥15 or immunocompromised → three

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Avoid live MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza** during pregnancy or severe immunosuppression
PCV15 → PPSV23: minimum 8 weeks if immunocompromised; mild illness/antibiotics need no deferral
Hesitancy → elicit concern, explain benefit, recommend clearly; refusal → document, revisit

table.title: Routine adult schedule
rows: Annual influenza; updated COVID-19 for all adults
Tdap once, then either every 10 years
PCV20/21 alone; PCV15 → PPSV23 after 1 year

anaphylaxis.name: Anaphylaxis
anaphylaxis.scope: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, biphasic reactions, epinephrine autoinjector, emergency airway management
anaphylaxis.core: Rapid multisystem reaction after exposure—or isolated hypotension or airway compromise after a known allergen—requires epinephrine immediately.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Foods, insect venom, antibiotics, latex; exercise can amplify food-triggered reactions
Asthma, prior severe reaction, mast-cell disorders; beta-blockers can complicate treatment

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Urticaria/angioedema + wheeze, stridor, hypotension, or severe GI symptoms**
Skin findings may be absent; hoarseness and tongue swelling predict airway danger
Biphasic recurrence after apparent resolution, especially after severe or undertreated episodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mast-cell/basophil mediators → vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchoconstriction; often IgE-mediated

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; never wait for tryptase or laboratory confirmation
Acute and baseline serum tryptase can support uncertain cases; normal results do not exclude anaphylaxis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg**, adult 0.3–0.5 mg, lateral thigh; repeat every 5–15 minutes
Supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress; oxygen, IV saline, early intubation for progressive obstruction
Refractory shock → monitored IV epinephrine infusion; beta-blocker-associated refractory reaction → glucagon
Albuterol for residual bronchospasm; antihistamines relieve itching only; steroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions
★ Monitor until resolved; **longer observation/admission** after hypotension, repeated epinephrine, or severe asthma

rows.label: Complications
items: Asphyxia, distributive shock, arrhythmia, hypoxic brain injury
IV epinephrine bolus errors → ischemia and dangerous dysrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prescribe **epinephrine autoinjector**, demonstrate technique, provide written action plan and allergy referral
Extra device for repeat-dose risk; avoidance, medical alert ID; venom immunotherapy after qualifying sting allergy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal episode: bradycardia, pallor, rapid improvement supine
Bradykinin angioedema: no itching/hives; ACE inhibitor or hereditary disease → airway, icatibant/C1 inhibitor

ankle-and-foot-injuries.name: Ankle and foot injuries
ankle-and-foot-injuries.scope: Lateral ankle sprain, Ottawa ankle and foot rules, RICE therapy, functional rehabilitation, Achilles tendon rupture, plantar fasciitis, calcaneal apophysitis
ankle-and-foot-injuries.core: Mechanism, focal tenderness, weight-bearing ability, and tendon function distinguish ankle sprain from fracture and overuse foot disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Inversion while plantarflexed, prior sprain, poor balance → lateral ligament injury
Running/jumping, sudden training increase, tight calves, obesity; fluoroquinolones/steroids increase tendon rupture risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Lateral swelling after inversion → **anterior talofibular ligament** injury most likely
Pain above ankle with external rotation/squeeze → syndesmotic sprain; recovery slower
Focal bony pain, deformity, neurovascular changes, or inability to bear weight → fracture evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ligament overstretch → microtears or disruption; tendon degeneration predisposes rupture
Repeated loading damages soft tissue; tendon degeneration reduces tensile strength

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Ankle pain + **posterior-edge/tip malleolar tenderness** → ankle radiographs
★ Midfoot pain + **navicular or fifth-metatarsal-base tenderness** → foot radiographs
Either region: inability to take four steps immediately and during evaluation also triggers corresponding radiographs
Examine skin, pulses, sensation; persistent focal pain despite normal films → reassess occult fracture

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sprain: **protection, ice, compression, elevation**, brief analgesia; early protected weight-bearing
Functional brace + range-of-motion, strength, proprioceptive rehabilitation; avoid prolonged routine immobilization
Displaced/open fracture or neurovascular compromise → urgent orthopedics; immobilize and keep non-weight-bearing

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic instability, recurrent sprains, osteochondral talar injury
Missed syndesmotic injury → prolonged disability; immobilization → stiffness, thrombosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Balance training and bracing** after prior sprain; gradual return when strength/function restored
Gradual training progression, supportive footwear, calf flexibility; avoid premature athletic return

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lisfranc injury: plantar ecchymosis, midfoot instability; weight-bearing radiographs
Septic arthritis: fever, marked passive-motion pain; aspirate joint

table.title: Heel disorders
rows: Pop, weak plantarflexion, abnormal Thompson test
First-step morning pain; medial plantar heel
Active child; posterior heel squeeze tenderness

ankle-and-foot-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic decision rules and rehabilitation principles.

antepartum-bleeding.name: Antepartum bleeding
antepartum-bleeding.scope: Placenta previa, placental abruption, vasa previa, uterine rupture, transabdominal ultrasound before digital exam, Kleihauer-Betke test, emergent cesarean delivery
antepartum-bleeding.core: Bleeding in later pregnancy requires immediate maternal stabilization and fetal assessment, followed by placental localization before any digital cervical examination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Previa: prior cesarean, multiparity; abruption: hypertension, cocaine, trauma, prior abruption
Vasa previa: velamentous cord, accessory placental lobe, IVF; rupture: uterine scar, obstructed labor

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Shock may exceed visible blood loss** with concealed abruption or internal hemorrhage
Assess uterine tone, pain, contractions, fetal tracing, membrane status; bleeding volume alone is unreliable

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maternal placental bleeding versus fetal vessel hemorrhage; vasa previa can rapidly exsanguinate fetus
Placental separation or uterine disruption compromises oxygen delivery independent of maternal external blood loss

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ CBC, type/crossmatch, coagulation studies including fibrinogen; continuous fetal monitoring if viable
★ **Ultrasound before digital examination**; transvaginal imaging safely clarifies placenta–cervix relationship
Normal ultrasound does not exclude abruption; suspected rupture is a clinical emergency
Rh-negative bleeding/trauma → Kleihauer–Betke or flow cytometry quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage for anti-D dosing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ ABCs, two large IVs, blood products when needed; **do not delay delivery for imaging if unstable**
Hemorrhage/fetal compromise → emergency cesarean; rupture → laparotomy, uterine repair or hysterectomy
Stable preterm previa → observation, pelvic rest, corticosteroids when eligible; planned cesarean before labor
Abruption: deliver if significant or compromised; vaginal birth possible when stable and imminent or fetal demise
Unsensitized Rh-negative patient → anti-D immunoglobulin; correct abruption-associated coagulopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, DIC, AKI, hysterectomy; fetal hypoxia, death, prematurity
Previa plus cesarean scar increases placenta accreta spectrum risk and operative hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP, avoid cocaine/tobacco; prenatal placental/cord localization and planned high-risk delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bloody show: small mucus-streaked bleeding with cervical change
Cervical lesion: contact bleeding, visible source on speculum examination

table.title: Critical distinctions
rows: Bleeding after rupture; sudden fetal bradycardia
Scarred uterus; lost station, fetal bradycardia

antepartum-bleeding.evidence: Not checked online; established obstetric hemorrhage teaching.

antipsychotics.name: Antipsychotics
antipsychotics.scope: First-generation vs second-generation, extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, QTc prolongation
antipsychotics.core: Dopamine-modulating drugs treat psychosis and mania; selection depends on motor, metabolic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and hematologic risks.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Psychosis, mania, severe agitation; **clozapine** for resistant schizophrenia or recurrent suicidality
FGA: mainly D2 antagonism; SGA: D2/5-HT2 effects, varying by agent

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Nigrostriatal blockade → movement disorders; tuberoinfundibular blockade → prolactin elevation
Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist; haloperidol high-potency FGA, chlorpromazine low-potency FGA

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Fever, **lead-pipe rigidity**, autonomic instability, high CK → NMS; stop drug, supportive ICU care
Severe NMS: dantrolene/bromocriptine; olanzapine/clozapine: weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia
Risperidone: ↑prolactin; ziprasidone: ↑QT; clozapine: neutropenia, myocarditis, ileus, seizures

rows.label: Avoid
items: Lewy body/Parkinson disease: severe sensitivity; specialist-selected quetiapine/clozapine if essential
Dementia: increased mortality; reserve for dangerous/severely distressing behavior after safer measures

rows.label: Interactions
items: Other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte depletion → torsades; sedatives/alcohol increase CNS depression

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Weight/BMI, BP, glucose/A1c, lipids; movement examinations; **ANC with clozapine**
ECG for cardiac/QT risks; prolactin when symptomatic; ask about bowel function

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia**; valbenazine/deutetrabenazine are VMAT2 inhibitors
Akathisia can mimic worsening agitation; increasing antipsychotic dose can worsen it
Low-potency FGAs: more orthostasis/anticholinergic effects; high-potency FGAs: more EPS

antipsychotics.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [FDA clozapine monitoring update](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-removes-risk-evaluation-and-mitigation-strategy-rems-program-antipsychotic-drug-clozapine); other effects established teaching.

aortic-dissection.name: Aortic dissection
aortic-dissection.core: Sudden maximal chest or back pain with vascular or neurologic deficits suggests aortic dissection, even without widened mediastinum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long-standing hypertension, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation
Marfan/vascular Ehlers-Danlos, pregnancy, cocaine, aortic instrumentation or aneurysm

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Abrupt severe pain**, pulse/BP asymmetry, syncope, focal neurologic deficit
New aortic regurgitation murmur; limb ischemia or abdominal pain from branch-vessel malperfusion
Hypotension suggests rupture, tamponade, severe regurgitation, or coronary involvement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intimal tear → blood separates medial layers, creating false lumen
Propagation compromises branch arteries or ruptures into pericardium/pleura

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable → **CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis**; unstable or unable to leave resuscitation → bedside TEE
Chest radiograph may show widened mediastinum but normal film does not exclude dissection
ECG/troponin may mimic MI; high suspicion requires aortic imaging before antithrombotics
Examine bilateral arm pressures, femoral pulses, neurologic status, renal function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV esmolol or labetalol** + opioid analgesia; target HR 60–80 and SBP <120 if perfusion maintained
Persistent hypertension after rate control → nicardipine; avoid vasodilator before beta blockade
★ **Avoid anticoagulation and thrombolysis** when dissection suspected
Tamponade from dissection → immediate surgical team; routine pericardiocentesis can worsen hemorrhage

rows.label: Complications
items: Aortic rupture, hemothorax, tamponade, MI, stroke, paraplegia, mesenteric/renal ischemia
Late aneurysmal dilation or recurrent dissection despite initial successful treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Lifelong **BP control and surveillance CTA/MRA**; beta-blocker-based regimen
Avoid heavy isometric lifting; screen first-degree relatives for familial aortopathy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute coronary syndrome: pressure-like pain, no pulse deficit; coexistence possible
PE: pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, right-heart strain
Esophageal rupture: vomiting followed by pain and subcutaneous emphysema

aortic-dissection.evidence: Not checked online; established aortic emergency principles.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.scope: Diagnosis, stepwise therapy, acute exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
asthma.core: Variable episodes of wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness from reversible expiratory airflow limitation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Atopy, family history, allergens, viral infections, smoke, occupational sensitizers
Exercise/cold air, aspirin-sensitive disease, nonselective beta-blockers; assess workplace symptom pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms; normal examination between attacks
★ **Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, rising PaCO2** → impending respiratory failure
Acute attack: low peak flow, accessory-muscle use, difficulty speaking

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction, mucus → variable obstruction and hyperresponsiveness
Persistent uncontrolled inflammation → remodeling with incompletely reversible airflow limitation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Spirometry**: obstruction with bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL in adults
Normal spirometry with suspicion → repeat during symptoms or methacholine challenge
Exercise challenge: postexercise FEV1 fall >10%; assess baseline control before isolated exercise diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **repeated inhaled albuterol + ipratropium**, oxygen, early systemic glucocorticoids
Severe poor response → IV magnesium; deterioration → intubation; avoid sedatives and routine antibiotics
Exercise symptoms → preexercise albuterol or prescribed ICS-formoterol; persistent symptoms → improve controller
Check technique/adherence before stepping up; uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS-LABA → phenotype-directed biologic referral

rows.label: Complications
items: Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, respiratory arrest
ICS → thrush/dysphonia; systemic steroids → osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Written action plan, trigger reduction, smoking cessation, spacer; rinse mouth after ICS
★ **No SABA-only treatment or LABA monotherapy**; current GINA differs from older intermittent-asthma teaching

rows.label: Mimics
items: Inducible laryngeal obstruction: inspiratory stridor, inspiratory flow-loop flattening
COPD: persistent obstruction, smoking history
HF: edema, elevated JVP, cardiac findings

atrioventricular-block.name: Atrioventricular block
atrioventricular-block.scope: First-degree, second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach), second-degree Mobitz type II, third-degree (complete) AV block, atropine, pacemaker indications
atrioventricular-block.core: Impaired atrial-to-ventricular conduction ranges from harmless delay to complete dissociation; symptoms and level of block determine urgency and pacing.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age-related conduction fibrosis, MI, beta blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, hyperkalemia
Lyme carditis, infiltrative disease, myocarditis, cardiac surgery; high vagal tone causes benign nodal delay

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, exertional intolerance, presyncope/syncope; cannon A waves with AV dissociation
★ Hypotension, confusion, ischemic discomfort, acute heart failure → **symptomatic unstable bradycardia**
Wide QRS and slow escape suggest distal disease; narrow escape may still be dangerous

rows.label: Pathophys
items: AV-nodal block often responds to vagal withdrawal; His–Purkinje failure risks unpredictable progression and asystole

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **12-lead ECG** establishes conduction pattern; continuous monitoring for significant block
Review drugs, electrolytes, ischemia; targeted Lyme testing with exposure; echo for structural disease
2:1 block cannot be labeled Mobitz I versus II from ratio alone; assess QRS and localization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → airway/oxygen if needed, IV access, **atropine** while preparing pacing
★ Atropine ineffective or distal high-grade block → **transcutaneous pacing**, then temporary transvenous pacing
Epinephrine/dopamine infusion can bridge to pacing; confirm electrical and mechanical capture
Stop AV-nodal blockers and correct reversible cause; do not wait for atropine in deteriorating infranodal disease
Permanent pacing for acquired Mobitz II, high-grade, or complete block without reversible cause, even asymptomatic

rows.label: Complications
items: Adams–Stokes syncope, low-output failure, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death
Pacemaker implantation → infection, pneumothorax, lead problems; prolonged RV pacing may impair LV function

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication review, ischemia/electrolyte treatment; asymptomatic first-degree or nodal Mobitz I usually observation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blocked premature atrial beat: early hidden P wave, noncompensatory pause
Sinus arrest: absent P waves during pause
AV dissociation from VT: ventricular tachycardia drives rhythm

table.title: ECG distinction
rows: Progressive PR lengthening, then dropped QRS
Constant conducted PR, sudden dropped QRS

carotid-artery-stenosis.name: Carotid artery stenosis
carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia; coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Prior neck radiation increases stenosis and surgical complexity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Amaurosis fugax**, contralateral weakness/numbness, or aphasia → symptomatic disease
Bruit may be incidental; loudness does not measure severity, complete occlusion may be silent
Isolated dizziness or syncope rarely represents carotid-territory ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture → artery-to-artery emboli; critical narrowing can reduce cerebral perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected stenosis or selected incidental bruit evaluation → **carotid duplex ultrasound**
CTA/MRA confirms anatomy before intervention; brain imaging evaluates neurologic deficits
★ **No routine screening** of asymptomatic general adults; bruit auscultation is an unreliable screen

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Post-revascularization hyperperfusion syndrome → headache, seizures, intracerebral hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms

table.title: Symptomatic ipsilateral stenosis
rows: Selected patients: age, sex, comorbidity matter

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.scope: Median nerve entrapment, pregnancy and endocrine risk factors, Phalen and Tinel tests, wrist splinting, corticosteroid injection, surgical release
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.core: Median nerve compression at the wrist causes nocturnal paresthesias in the thumb, index, middle, and radial ring fingers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pregnancy/fluid retention, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis
Forceful repetitive hand activity, wrist trauma; dialysis-associated amyloid in selected patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Shaking hand relieves symptoms; driving or sustained wrist flexion aggravates symptoms
★ **Thenar weakness/atrophy**, dropping objects, impaired thumb opposition → advanced nerve injury
Central palm sensation usually spared because palmar cutaneous branch bypasses tunnel
Bilateral symptoms common; isolated little-finger symptoms argue against median neuropathy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Raised pressure beneath transverse carpal ligament → median nerve ischemia/demyelination
Long-standing compression progresses to axonal loss and persistent motor impairment

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical history + **Phalen/Tinel or carpal compression** findings support clinical diagnosis
Phalen: sustained wrist flexion; Tinel: percussion over median nerve reproduces distal paresthesia
★ **Nerve-conduction studies/EMG** for atypical presentation, severity assessment, or uncertain diagnosis before surgery
Targeted TSH/glucose testing when systemic disease suspected; routine wrist imaging unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Mild/moderate → **neutral-position wrist splint at night**, ergonomic modification
Local corticosteroid injection for persistent symptoms or short-term relief; pregnancy often resolves postpartum
★ Severe deficit, denervation, or failed conservative care → **surgical carpal tunnel release**
NSAIDs do not relieve the underlying compression; avoid repeated ineffective analgesic-only management

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent sensory loss and thenar wasting if severe compression persists
Injection → transient hyperglycemia, rare nerve injury; surgery → scar pain or incomplete release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce prolonged wrist flexion/extension and forceful vibration; adjust workstation and tools
Manage contributing endocrine/inflammatory disease; reassess worsening motor function promptly

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical radiculopathy: neck pain, dermatomal weakness/reflex changes
Ulnar neuropathy: little finger/ulnar ring symptoms, interosseous weakness
Pronator syndrome: proximal forearm pain with palmar sensory involvement

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

cataracts.name: Cataracts
cataracts.scope: Nuclear sclerotic, cortical, posterior subcapsular, painless vision loss, night driving glare, halos around lights, loss of red reflex, phacoemulsification
cataracts.core: Progressive lens clouding causes painless blurred vision, glare, and impaired daily activities; surgery restores optical clarity.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Aging, diabetes, smoking, ultraviolet exposure, ocular trauma
Chronic glucocorticoids and radiation; congenital cases: genetic disease or intrauterine infection

rows.label: Clues
items: Night driving difficulty, halos around headlights, faded colors, reduced contrast
★ **Diminished red reflex**, lens opacity; monocular diplopia possible
No afferent pupillary defect from uncomplicated lens disease; pain/redness suggests another diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Lens protein aggregation and altered hydration scatter light before it reaches the retina
Diabetes: sorbitol accumulation accelerates osmotic lens damage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Slit-lamp examination** after visual acuity and refraction; dilated fundus examination
Assess retinal disease before surgery; ultrasound when dense opacity blocks fundus visualization
Infant leukocoria → urgent ophthalmology; exclude retinoblastoma rather than assuming cataract

rows.label: Tx
items: Early functional preservation: updated glasses, brighter lighting, glare reduction
★ Function-limiting impairment → **phacoemulsification + intraocular lens**; no visual-acuity threshold required
Congenital visually significant opacity → prompt treatment to prevent deprivation amblyopia

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated severe disease: falls, driving impairment; neglected hypermature lens: inflammation or secondary glaucoma
Surgical: endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, cystoid macular edema
★ Later recurrent haze: **posterior capsule opacification → Nd:YAG capsulotomy**

rows.label: Prevention
items: UV-blocking eyewear, smoking cessation, glucose control; minimize unnecessary steroid exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Open-angle glaucoma: peripheral field loss, optic disc cupping
Macular degeneration: central distortion, drusen or retinal neovascularization
Acute angle closure: painful red eye, nausea, fixed mid-dilated pupil

table.title: Lens opacity patterns
rows: Central yellowing; myopic shift, temporary reading improvement
Steroids; near vision and bright-light difficulty

cataracts.evidence: Not checked online; established ophthalmology teaching.

caustic-ingestion.name: Caustic ingestion
caustic-ingestion.scope: Acid and alkali ingestion, airway assessment, contraindications to emesis or neutralization, early esophagogastroduodenoscopy within 24 hours, stricture complications
caustic-ingestion.core: Corrosive ingestion can burn the airway and gastrointestinal tract; a normal mouth examination does not exclude deep injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young children: accidental household cleaner exposure; adults: intentional large-volume ingestion
Drain cleaners, oven cleaners, industrial acids; concentration and contact duration determine severity

rows.label: Clues
items: Drooling, odynophagia, dysphagia, vomiting, hematemesis, chest or abdominal pain
★ **Stridor, hoarseness, respiratory distress** → threatened airway
Severe tenderness, rigidity, fever, shock → transmural necrosis or perforation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alkali: liquefactive necrosis, deep esophageal penetration; acid: coagulative necrosis, often gastric injury
Both agents can injure the entire upper gastrointestinal tract; eschar provides incomplete protection

rows.label: Dx
items: Identify substance, concentration, amount, time; poison control consultation
★ Stable symptomatic/significant exposure → **EGD within 24 hours** for injury grading
Suspected perforation/necrosis → contrast CT chest/abdomen and surgery consultation; avoid diagnostic endoscopy if perforated
CBC, electrolytes, renal function, lactate, blood gas; normal labs cannot exclude injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Airway first**; early controlled intubation with direct visualization when swelling progresses
NPO, IV crystalloid, analgesia; surgical treatment for perforation or full-thickness necrosis
★ **No emesis, neutralization, gastric lavage, or activated charcoal**; additional burns or heat generation
Avoid blind NG placement; no routine corticosteroids or prophylactic antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Mediastinitis, peritonitis, hemorrhage, fistula; delayed esophageal stricture or gastric outlet obstruction
Long-term esophageal squamous cell carcinoma risk; strictures may require repeated dilation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Locked storage in original labeled containers; never transfer chemicals into beverage bottles
Intentional ingestion → psychiatric assessment after stabilization; swallowing/nutrition follow-up after severe injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal foreign body: discrete obstruction on history or imaging
Pill esophagitis: medication exposure, focal ulceration without extensive chemical burns

caustic-ingestion.evidence: Not checked online; established toxicology teaching.

cervicitis-pid.name: Cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease
cervicitis-pid.core: Sexually active patient with mucopurulent discharge or postcoital bleeding; ascending infection adds pelvic pain, sometimes an adnexal abscess.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <25, new/multiple partners, inconsistent condoms, prior STI
IUD-associated PID risk concentrated within first 3 weeks after insertion

rows.label: Clues
items: Cervical friability, easily induced endocervical bleeding; infection sometimes asymptomatic
Dyspareunia, fever; severe unilateral pain/adnexal mass → **tubo-ovarian abscess**
Peritonitis, shock → rupture; RUQ pain → Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GC/CT ascend cervix → endometrium/tubes; PID often polymicrobial, including anaerobes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test** first; vaginal/cervical or urine **GC/CT NAAT**; HIV/syphilis testing
★ Pelvic pain + **cervical motion, uterine, OR adnexal tenderness** → presumptive PID; no confirmation delay
Negative cervical NAAT does not exclude upper-tract infection; normal discharge/no vaginal leukocytes argues against PID
**Transvaginal US** for abscess or diagnostic uncertainty; routine laparoscopy unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Cervicitis: empiric GC/CT coverage IF high risk/unreliable follow-up; otherwise await NAAT
★ Admit IF **pregnant, abscess, severe illness**, oral intolerance, uncertain surgical diagnosis, or failure by 72 h
Abscess rupture → emergency surgery; persistent abscess after 48–72 h antibiotics → drainage
Pregnant chlamydia → **azithromycin**, avoid doxycycline; retain IUD initially, reassess if no improvement

rows.label: Complications
items: Tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain; abscess → sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from prior **60 days**; abstain until courses completed, partners treated, symptoms resolved
Retest GC/CT at 3 months; pregnant chlamydia → test of cure at 4 weeks
Annual GC/CT screening: sexually active women <25, older women with risks; condoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, no confirmed intrauterine pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt unilateral pain, vomiting; Doppler flow may persist
Appendicitis: migrating RLQ pain, CT appendiceal inflammation

table.title: Antibiotic branches
rows: Ceftriaxone; add CT regimen unless excluded
Oral drugs 14 days; ceftriaxone once IM outpatient

chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.name: Chromosomal and genetic disorders
chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.scope: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (45,X0), Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), Fragile X syndrome (FMR1 trinucleotide repeat), Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes, DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion)
chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.core: Recognize syndromic combinations of growth, cognition, gonadal function, dysmorphism, and congenital malformations; confirm with the correct genetic test.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced maternal age: meiotic nondisjunction; balanced parental translocation: recurrent aneuploid pregnancy
Family expansion history: repeat disorders; many microdeletions and sex-chromosome abnormalities arise de novo

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Down**: hypotonia, upslanting fissures, single palmar crease, AV septal defect
DiGeorge: conotruncal defect, cleft palate, absent thymus, hypocalcemic tetany

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **Genomic imprinting**: parent-specific expression; deletion or uniparental disomy can disrupt the active copy
22q11 deletion disrupts pharyngeal pouch development → T-cell deficiency and hypoparathyroidism

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected Down → **karyotype confirms trisomy 21**; prenatal screening alone never establishes diagnosis
Microarray: microdeletion; targeted repeat analysis: fragile X; methylation testing: imprinting disorders
Down: assess heart, hearing, vision, thyroid; DiGeorge: calcium and lymphocyte subsets

rows.label: Tx
items: Early developmental services, speech support; repair congenital defects
Turner: growth hormone then estrogen/progestin; Klinefelter: testosterone after endocrine assessment
Prader-Willi: supervised food access; Angelman: seizure management; DiGeorge: calcium and infection management

rows.label: Complications
items: Down: duodenal atresia, leukemia, early Alzheimer disease, atlantoaxial instability
Turner: coarctation, bicuspid valve, aortic dissection; Klinefelter: infertility, breast cancer
Prader-Willi: severe obesity; DiGeorge: severe infections and later psychiatric disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**: recurrence depends on nondisjunction, translocation, imprinting mechanism, or repeat expansion
Avoid live vaccines with severe T-cell deficiency; use irradiated blood for profound immunodeficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Noonan syndrome: Turner-like habitus with normal chromosomes; either sex
Congenital hypothyroidism: hypotonia and delayed development; abnormal newborn thyroid screen

table.title: Distinctive genotype–phenotype pairs
rows: Short female, webbed neck, streak ovaries
Tall male, small firm testes, gynecomastia

chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established genetics teaching.

chronic-venous-insufficiency.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
chronic-venous-insufficiency.scope: Varicose veins, stasis dermatitis, venous stasis ulcers, superficial thrombophlebitis, post-thrombotic syndrome
chronic-venous-insufficiency.core: Venous hypertension produces dependent edema, hemosiderin pigmentation, and shallow medial ankle ulcers that improve with elevation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior DVT, obesity, pregnancy, prolonged standing, older age, family history
Reduced calf-muscle pumping from immobility; previous leg trauma or venous surgery

rows.label: Clues
items: Aching/heaviness worsened by standing; varicosities, pitting swelling, preserved pedal pulses
Eczematous itching, lipodermatosclerosis, inverted champagne-bottle leg contour
★ **Irregular, exudative gaiter-region wound**; bilateral erythema without systemic illness favors stasis dermatitis
Superficial thrombophlebitis: focal erythema over a tender palpable venous cord

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Valve failure or outflow obstruction → reflux, capillary leakage, chronic inflammation
Post-thrombotic syndrome: residual obstruction and valvular injury following DVT

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous duplex ultrasound** evaluates reflux and obstruction; clinical examination often establishes diagnosis
★ **Ankle-brachial index before compression** when PAD suspected; <0.5 → avoid sustained compression
Nonhealing or atypical ulcer → biopsy for malignancy; sudden unilateral worsening → evaluate acute DVT
New superficial cord → assess clot length, proximity to deep junction, associated DVT

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adequate arterial inflow → **compression bandaging/stockings + leg elevation**; walking activates calf pump
Ulcers: saline cleansing, moist absorbent dressings, debridement when needed
Stasis dermatitis: emollients plus short-course topical corticosteroid on intact inflamed skin
Symptomatic superficial reflux → endovenous ablation; moderate arterial disease → specialist-guided reduced compression
No antibiotics for colonization alone; cellulitis → systemic antibiotics; no routine diuretics without volume overload

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent ulceration, cellulitis, contact dermatitis; superficial clot can extend into deep veins
Chronic wounds rarely undergo squamous malignant transformation; new growth or bleeding warrants biopsy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Weight reduction, regular mobility, avoid prolonged dependent posture
Long-term compression after ulcer healing reduces recurrence; moisturize skin and treat venous reflux

rows.label: Mimics
items: Arterial ulcer: painful punched-out toes/lateral ankle, cool foot, weak pulses
Neuropathic ulcer: plantar pressure points, sensory loss, callus
Lymphedema: dorsal foot/toe swelling, later nonpitting thickened skin

table.title: Superficial thrombosis treatment
rows: Short distal segment, no high-risk features
≥5 cm long, >3 cm from deep junction

chronic-venous-insufficiency.evidence: Thrombosis checked 2026-10-30: [SVS/AVF/AVLS 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11523430/); wound care established teaching.

clostridioides-difficile-infection.name: Clostridioides difficile infection
clostridioides-difficile-infection.scope: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, toxic megacolon, pseudomembranous colitis, NAAT vs EIA stool toxin testing, oral fidaxomicin, oral vancomycin, fulminant colitis
clostridioides-difficile-infection.core: Recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure followed by watery diarrhea suggests toxin-mediated colitis; ileus can conceal fulminant disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins; older age, hospitalization, immunosuppression
Prior infection and unnecessary acid suppression increase susceptibility or recurrence

rows.label: Clues
items: Abdominal cramps, fever, leukocytosis; severe disease may cause AKI and hypoalbuminemia
★ **Hypotension, ileus, or megacolon** defines fulminant infection; diarrhea may disappear

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Antibiotic disruption of microbiota permits spore-forming bacilli to proliferate
Toxins damage colonic epithelium → inflammation and pseudomembranes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Test **unformed stool** with ≥3 unexplained stools/24 hours; exclude laxative effect
NAAT detects toxigenic genes, not active toxin; positive results can represent colonization
Toxin EIA is less sensitive; multistep GDH/NAAT plus toxin improves clinical specificity
No test of cure; abdominal imaging for distention, toxicity, or suspected perforation

rows.label: Tx
items: Stop inciting antibiotic when possible; replace fluids/electrolytes, avoid antimotility drugs in severe colitis
★ Initial nonfulminant infection: **oral fidaxomicin** preferred; oral vancomycin acceptable, usually 10 days
★ Fulminant: **high-dose oral/NG vancomycin + IV metronidazole**; add rectal vancomycin with ileus
Shock, perforation, worsening organ failure → urgent surgical consultation
Recurrence: fidaxomicin or tapered/pulsed vancomycin; multiple recurrences → screened microbiota-based treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Toxic megacolon, perforation, sepsis, recurrent infection
Severe classification: WBC >15,000/µL or creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL; different from fulminant criteria

rows.label: Prevention
items: Contact precautions, gloves/gown, soap-and-water handwashing, sporicidal surface cleaning
Antibiotic stewardship; no screening/treatment of asymptomatic carriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Laxative-associated diarrhea: medication timing, no inflammatory syndrome
IBD flare: chronic relapsing course; test for coinfection before escalating immunosuppression

contraception.name: Contraception
contraception.scope: Combined oral contraceptives, progestin-only pills, implant, intrauterine devices, tubal sterilization
contraception.core: Choose contraception through shared decisions about efficacy, bleeding, reversibility, adherence, and estrogen-related vascular risk.

rows.label: Who
items: Anyone seeking pregnancy prevention; adolescents and nulliparous patients can use IUDs or implants

rows.label: Schedule
items: Pills daily; implants/IUDs provide years of protection; replacement interval depends on product
★ Emergency contraception ≤**5 days**: copper IUD/ulipristal; levonorgestrel pills sooner preferred

rows.label: Special groups
items: Breastfeeding or estrogen contraindication → progestin-only method or copper IUD
Current breast cancer → copper IUD; avoid hormonal methods
Progestin-only pills: daily timing crucial; norethindrone less forgiving than drospirenone

rows.label: Choice
items: Combined pills: suppress ovulation, improve acne/cramps, reduce endometrial/ovarian cancer risk
★ **LARC** minimizes adherence failures; condoms add STI protection
Tubal sterilization: permanent; counsel regret, alternatives, surgical risk, ectopic risk after failure

rows.label: Contraindications
items: ★ Estrogen: **migraine with aura, thrombophilia/high-risk VTE**, severe hypertension, early postpartum
Smoking age ≥35: combined methods usually avoid; ≥15 cigarettes/day → absolute contraindication
IUD: pregnancy, cervicitis/PID, distorted cavity; copper: also Wilson disease

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Same-day STI screening need not delay insertion without cervicitis; prior PID alone permits IUD
Sterilization: voluntary informed consent; no required partner approval, parity, or marital status
After ulipristal, wait 5 days before progestin; backup contraception needed after hormonal restart

copd.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
copd.scope: Stable COPD, acute exacerbation (AECOPD), oxygen-induced hypercapnia, noninvasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP), indications for intubation, bronchodilators and glucocorticoids
copd.core: Persistent airflow obstruction after inhalational exposure causes progressive exertional dyspnea and episodic infectious or inflammatory exacerbations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Tobacco, biomass smoke, occupational dusts; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with early/basilar emphysema

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic cough/sputum, prolonged expiration, wheeze, hyperinflation
★ **Somnolence, exhaustion, silent chest, worsening acidosis** → impending respiratory failure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Small-airway inflammation + alveolar destruction → expiratory collapse, air trapping, impaired diffusion
Excess oxygen worsens CO₂ retention mainly through V/Q mismatch and Haldane effect

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Postbronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.70** confirms persistent obstruction in compatible clinical setting
Exacerbation: pulse oximetry; ABG for severe distress/altered mentation; radiograph for pneumonia, edema, pneumothorax
Consider ECG, troponin, BNP, or PE evaluation when symptoms exceed expected exacerbation pattern

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **albuterol + ipratropium**, prednisone for 5 days; titrate oxygen to 88–92%
Antibiotics: purulence + increased dyspnea/sputum volume, or ventilatory support; doxycycline/azithromycin options
★ Hypercapnic acidosis, pH ≤7.35 → **BiPAP** unless aspiration risk, arrest, instability, inability to cooperate
Intubate for failed NIV, severe encephalopathy, refractory hypoxemia, or inability to protect airway
Long-term oxygen if stable PaO₂ ≤55 or saturation ≤88%; selected cor pulmonale/polycythemia with PaO₂ 56–59

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, secondary polycythemia, cachexia
Pneumonia risk with inhaled steroids; ventilation → dynamic hyperinflation, auto-PEEP, barotrauma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Smoking cessation**, influenza/COVID/pneumococcal/RSV vaccination when eligible, pulmonary rehabilitation
Check inhaler technique/adherence; offer alpha-1 antitrypsin testing at least once

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: variable symptoms and reversible obstruction
Heart failure: orthopnea, edema, vascular congestion; bronchiectasis: copious sputum, dilated bronchi

table.title: Stable inhaled treatment
rows: Exacerbations with eosinophilia or concurrent asthma

copd.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [GOLD 2026](https://goldcopd.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/GOLD-REPORT-2026-v1.3-8Dec2025_WMV2.pdf); acute ventilatory care: established teaching.

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age, family history; vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease
Anticholinergics, sedatives, alcohol, hearing loss, sleep apnea may worsen cognition

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving
Personality, language, executive, visuospatial, memory, motor symptoms help establish phenotype
Abrupt change, fluctuating attention, fever, focal deficits → evaluate acute superimposed illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alzheimer: amyloid plaques/tau tangles; Lewy/Parkinson: alpha-synuclein; vascular disease: ischemic neuronal injury
Frontotemporal degeneration affects frontal/anterior temporal networks, often before typical late-life onset

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval with preserved independence; MCI: objective deficit without loss of independent function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy disease**
Early biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer: specialist-selected antiamyloid drugs; baseline/serial MRI for ARIA

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity
Exercise, hearing correction, social engagement, vascular risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Delirium: hours–days, impaired attention, fluctuating awareness
Depression: prominent distress, variable effort, potentially reversible cognitive deficits
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-first decline, incontinence, ventriculomegaly; tap test may predict shunt response

table.title: Phenotype clues
rows: Insidious episodic-memory decline, later multidomain deficits
Stroke-related or stepwise decline, focal findings
Early hallucinations, fluctuation, REM behavior, parkinsonism
Early disinhibition/apathy or progressive aphasia; memory spared
Established motor disease >1 year before dementia

dementia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [Alzheimer's Association diagnostic guidance 2024](https://www.alz.org/news/2024/clinical-practice-guideline-evaluation-alzheimers), [NICE dementia](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations/); established subtype teaching.

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; depression may present as somatic complaints

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, stress responses, and neuroplasticity
Antidepressant benefit develops over weeks despite early changes in neurotransmitter availability

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
PHQ-9 quantifies severity; interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger → **continuous observation and psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal psychotherapy; moderate/severe: SSRI such as sertraline + psychotherapy
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid eating disorders; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation, useful with anorexia/insomnia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after starting/changing drugs, family support with consent
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; depressive cognitive impairment often prominent complaints and variable effort
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

dermatophyte-infections.name: Dermatophyte infections
dermatophyte-infections.scope: Tinea capitis, tinea corporis, tinea pedis, tinea cruris, onychomycosis, potassium hydroxide preparation, oral and topical antifungals
dermatophyte-infections.core: Keratin-invading fungi cause scaly skin lesions or infected hair/nails; the anatomic site determines topical versus systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Warm humid conditions, occlusive footwear, shared showers, wrestling, infected animals or contacts
Diabetes, immunosuppression; childhood favors scalp infection; nail disease increases with age

rows.label: Clues
items: Pruritus and peripheral scaling; steroid exposure may distort borders and suppress inflammation
★ **Boggy tender scalp plaque** → kerion; inflammatory disease risks permanent scarring alopecia
Interdigital maceration/fissures can become bacterial entry sites

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton digest keratin in stratum corneum, hair, and nails
Follicular/deep involvement prevents topical agents from reaching the infected reservoir

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **KOH preparation of active edge** → branching septate hyphae; obtain before systemic treatment when uncertain
Scalp: hair/plucked scale microscopy and culture; nail: clipping KOH, PAS, or fungal culture
Wood lamp detects only selected organisms; negative fluorescence does not exclude tinea
Refractory/widespread infection → reassess diagnosis, adherence, resistance; fungal culture can guide further care

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Limited skin disease → **topical terbinafine** or clotrimazole; continue beyond clinical clearing
★ Hair infection → **oral griseofulvin or terbinafine**; adjunct selenium sulfide/ketoconazole shampoo reduces spread
Nail infection → confirm fungus, then oral terbinafine; baseline liver assessment; counsel slow regrowth
Avoid topical corticosteroid monotherapy or steroid-antifungal combinations; extensive disease may require oral antifungal

rows.label: Complications
items: Secondary cellulitis, persistent nail dystrophy, recurrent infection from untreated reservoirs
Oral antifungals: hepatotoxicity, drug interactions; griseofulvin contraindicated during pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Keep feet dry**, change socks, avoid shared towels/combs, disinfect sports gear
Treat symptomatic contacts/pets and coexisting foot disease; avoid barefoot communal-shower exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Candida intertrigo: satellite pustules, scrotal involvement
Psoriasis: sharply demarcated plaques, nail pitting; alopecia areata: smooth nonscaly patches

table.title: Site clues
rows: Broken hairs, black dots, patchy alopecia
Annular plaque, advancing border, central clearing
Thick yellow brittle nail, subungual debris

dermatophyte-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatophyte diagnosis and site-based treatment.

diabetic-neuropathy.name: Diabetic neuropathy
diabetic-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, foot ulcer prevention, pharmacotherapy (duloxetine, pregabalin, TCAs)
diabetic-neuropathy.core: Diabetes damages sensory, motor, and autonomic nerves; identify the pattern, exclude additional causes, relieve pain, and protect insensate feet.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long diabetes duration, chronic hyperglycemia, smoking, kidney disease, dyslipidemia
Alcohol excess and metformin-associated B12 deficiency may coexist and worsen symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Acute asymmetric weakness, marked motor loss**, or rapid progression → investigate another cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Metabolic and microvascular injury damages peripheral axons; longest nerves affected first
Loss of protective sensation plus deformity/ischemia → repetitive unnoticed trauma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **10-g monofilament + vibration/pinprick/temperature**, ankle reflexes; inspect skin, deformity, pulses
Screen at type 2 diagnosis, 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, then at least annually
Check B12, TSH, renal function when evaluating neuropathy; consider serum electrophoresis if unexplained
Atypical pattern → nerve conduction studies; gastroparesis → exclude obstruction, gastric-emptying study
New third-nerve palsy → urgent vascular imaging; pupil sparing cannot reliably exclude aneurysm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain → **duloxetine or pregabalin**; gabapentin or selected TCAs alternatives
Avoid TCAs with arrhythmia, urinary retention, frailty; avoid opioids for routine chronic neuropathic pain
Improve glycemic management; no drug reliably restores established sensory loss
Orthostasis → hydration, compression, medication review; persistent symptoms → midodrine
Gastroparesis → small low-fat meals, short-term metoclopramide; erectile dysfunction → sildenafil unless nitrates

rows.label: Complications
items: Painless ulcers, osteomyelitis, amputation, Charcot arthropathy
Falls, burns, painless MI; metoclopramide → tardive dyskinesia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection, protective footwear**, podiatry for callus/nail care; never walk barefoot
Regular foot exams, smoking cessation; warm swollen neuropathic foot → off-load and assess Charcot/infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: posterior column findings, elevated methylmalonic acid
Radiculopathy: dermatomal unilateral pain with root-specific weakness
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses, ischemic skin changes

diabetic-neuropathy.evidence: Not checked online; established diabetes neuropathy screening and management teaching.

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Burning/numb feet, reduced vibration and ankle reflexes
Orthostasis, tachycardia, gastroparesis, bladder/sexual dysfunction, hypoglycemia unawareness
Acute isolated nerve deficit; often reversible

diagnostic-test-accuracy.name: Diagnostic test accuracy
diagnostic-test-accuracy.scope: Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, likelihood ratios, cut-off changes
diagnostic-test-accuracy.core: Diagnostic accuracy: classification performance against a reference standard; distinguish detection ability from the probability that a result reflects disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: TP/FP: diseased/nondiseased testing positive; FN/TN: diseased/nondiseased testing negative

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ ↑Prevalence → **↑PPV, ↓NPV**; sensitivity/specificity unchanged if disease spectrum unchanged
★ Positive above threshold: **lower cutoff → ↑sensitivity, ↓specificity**; raising cutoff reverses
LR+ >10 rules in strongly; LR− <0.1 rules out strongly

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Pretest odds = p/(1−p); **posttest odds = pretest odds × LR**
Posttest probability = odds/(1+odds); pretest 20%, LR+ 4 → odds 1 → 50%
Parallel tests, either positive → ↑sensitivity; serial tests, both positive → ↑specificity

rows.label: Compare
items: ROC: sensitivity versus 1−specificity; AUC 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Sensitive negative** helps exclude; specific positive helps confirm; neither absolute
Case-control sampling → PPV/NPV unrepresentative without population prevalence
Verification bias: reference testing only selected results → distorted accuracy

diagnostic-test-accuracy.evidence: Established statistical definitions; no guideline-dependent recommendation.

diverticular-disease.name: Diverticular disease
diverticular-disease.scope: Diverticulosis, acute diverticulitis, complicated diverticulitis (abscess, perforation, fistula), CT imaging, antibiotic therapy
